fields.title: 1 Samuel
fields.subtitle: Shemuel Alef, “The First Book of Samuel”
fields.description: The book in which Israel gets a king, and learns what kind of king God wants. It opens with Hannah pouring out her soul in the sanctuary at Shiloh and singing of a God who lifts the poor from the dust, and with the boy Samuel answering in the night, “Speak, for your servant is listening.” Then the ark captured and Dagon fallen on his face, the people demanding a king like all the nations, and tall Saul, who began well and could not obey. And then the shepherd boy no one sent for, because “the LORD looks at the heart”: David with his sling before Goliath, Jonathan’s friendship, Saul’s spear, the years in caves and deserts, and the LORD’s anointed spared twice by the man who would take his throne. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of 1 Samuel about?
qa.answer: The change from the time of the judges to the monarchy in Israel, told through three lives. Samuel, born in answer to his mother Hannah’s prayer, becomes prophet and the last of the judges (chapters 1–7). The people demand a king, and Samuel anoints Saul, who is later rejected for disobedience (chapters 8–15). God then chooses David, a shepherd from Bethlehem, who defeats Goliath, is befriended by Saul’s son Jonathan, and is hunted by the jealous Saul until Saul dies in battle on Mount Gilboa (chapters 16–31).

qa.question: Who wrote 1 Samuel, and when?
qa.answer: The book does not name its author, and Samuel dies before it ends (25:1). 1 Chronicles 29:29 mentions records kept by the prophets Samuel, Nathan and Gad, and Jewish tradition held that Samuel wrote the part up to his death, with the rest completed by others. Many scholars think the book drew on several older sources and reached its final form, together with 2 Samuel, as part of a longer history in the time of the kings or later. 1 and 2 Samuel were originally a single book.

qa.question: Why did God reject Saul as king?
qa.answer: Because he would not obey the LORD’s command. In 1 Samuel 13 he offered a sacrifice himself instead of waiting for Samuel, and in chapter 15 he spared the Amalekite king and the best of the livestock that God had told him to devote to destruction, then claimed he had obeyed. Samuel told him that “to obey is better than sacrifice” (15:22) and that because he had rejected the word of the LORD, the LORD had rejected him as king. God chose instead “a man after his own heart” (13:14).

qa.question: Did God change his mind about Saul?
qa.answer: 1 Samuel 15 says twice that the LORD regretted making Saul king (15:11, 15:35), and in between Samuel says that God “will not lie or change his mind, for he is not a mortal, that he should change his mind” (15:29). Most interpreters read the two together: God is not fickle or caught by surprise as human beings are, and his purposes stand; yet he truly responds to human choices, and his grief over Saul’s disobedience is real. Theologians differ on how best to describe this, but the chapter itself holds both truths side by side.

qa.question: What does “the LORD looks at the heart” mean?
qa.answer: When Samuel came to Bethlehem to anoint one of Jesse’s sons, he was impressed by the eldest, Eliab, but God told him: “Pay no attention to his looks or to how tall he is… A person looks at what is there for the eyes, but the LORD looks at the heart” (16:7). God chose instead the youngest son, David, who had been left out with the sheep. The saying sums up a theme that runs through the book, from Hannah’s song onward: God lifts up the humble and is not impressed by outward strength, as Saul, the tallest man in Israel, and Goliath both show.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. “LORD” in capitals stands for God’s personal name, and Hannah’s song is set out line by line as poetry. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
But the LORD said to Samuel, “Pay no attention to his looks or to how tall he is, because I have rejected him. The LORD does not see in the way a person sees. A person looks at what is there for the eyes, but the LORD looks at the heart.”

— 1 Samuel 16:7

1 Samuel is a book about change. It begins in the world of Judges, with a priest growing old and blind at a sanctuary in Shiloh, his sons abusing their office, and “the word of the LORD was rare in those days”. It ends with Israel a kingdom, its first king dead on a battlefield, and a young man from Bethlehem waiting in exile for the throne God has promised him.

Three lives hold the book together. Samuel, the child of a mother’s prayer, who becomes prophet, priest and the last of the judges. Saul, the tall, handsome king the people asked for, who began well and ended at a medium’s house the night before his death. And David, the shepherd boy whom no one thought to send for, the man after God’s own heart. Their stories overlap and pass on from one to the next, and between them they tell how God gave his people a king, and what kind of king he wanted.

One book in two

1 and 2 Samuel were originally a single book, named after the prophet who dominates its first half: in Hebrew, Shemuel. The ancient Greek translators divided it in two, along with Kings, and called the four “Books of Kingdoms”; Christian Bibles have followed the division ever since, and Hebrew Bibles since the late Middle Ages. Samuel himself dies before the end of 1 Samuel, but the name is fitting. It was Samuel who anointed both of Israel’s first kings, and his words over them shape all that follows.

The book falls into three overlapping parts:

  • Samuel (chapters 1–7). Hannah’s prayer, Samuel’s call, the fall of Eli’s house, the capture and return of the ark, and Samuel’s leadership at Mizpah.
  • Saul (chapters 8–15). The people’s demand for a king, Saul’s anointing and early victories, and his rejection for disobedience.
  • Saul and David (chapters 16–31). David anointed in secret, the victory over Goliath, Jonathan’s friendship, Saul’s jealousy, David’s years as a fugitive, and Saul’s death on Mount Gilboa.

Hannah’s prayer

The book does not open with a king or a prophet. It opens with a woman who cannot have children, mocked every year by her husband’s other wife as they go up to the sanctuary. Hannah’s husband loves her, but asks, “Do I not mean more to you than ten sons?” She goes to the tent of the LORD and prays so intensely that only her lips move, and the priest Eli thinks she is drunk. Her answer is one of the great descriptions of prayer: “I have been pouring out my soul before the LORD.”

She vows that if God gives her a son, she will give him back to the LORD for his whole life. A son is born, and she names him Samuel, “I asked the LORD for him.” When he is weaned, she brings him to Shiloh and leaves him with Eli. And then she sings:

The LORD makes some poor and others rich; he humbles, and he also exalts. He lifts the poor up out of the dust and raises those in need from the ash heap, to seat them with nobles and give them a throne of honor as their own. For the pillars of the earth belong to the LORD; on them he has set the world.

— 1 Samuel 2:7–8

Hannah’s song is the overture to the whole book. Its theme is reversal: the proud brought low, the humble lifted up, “for no one wins by strength.” That is the story of Eli’s house and Samuel, of Saul and David, of Goliath and the shepherd boy. And it ends on a word no one in Israel has yet used of a ruler: God “will grant strength to his king and raise high the horn of his anointed.” There is no king yet. The word “anointed”, mashiach, is the word that will become “Messiah”. More than a thousand years later, another woman, pregnant with a promised son, would sing a song so like Hannah’s that readers have heard the one in the other ever since: “He has pulled the mighty down from their thrones and raised up the lowly.”

“Speak, for your servant is listening”

Eli’s sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are priests at Shiloh, and they treat the offerings of God’s people with contempt. “Now Eli’s sons were worthless men; they did not know the LORD.” Eli rebukes them feebly and does nothing. Against that background the boy Samuel grows, “and both the LORD and the people were pleased with him”, words Luke would echo of the boy Jesus.

One night, as Samuel lies in the sanctuary near the ark, a voice calls his name. Three times he runs to Eli, and three times Eli sends him back, until the old priest realises who is calling, and tells him how to answer:

The LORD came and took his stand there, and called as before, “Samuel! Samuel!” Samuel replied, “Speak, for your servant is listening.”

— 1 Samuel 3:10

The message Samuel receives is hard: judgement on Eli’s house. But the chapter ends with the word of the LORD no longer rare. Samuel grows up, “and the LORD was with him; he did not let any of his words fall to the ground.” All Israel, “from Dan to Beersheba”, knows that there is a prophet in the land again.

The ark and the glory

Chapters 4–6 can seem a detour, since Samuel himself is not mentioned in most of them. But they teach something Israel needed to learn. Beaten by the Philistines, the elders send for the ark of the covenant, thinking that if they carry it into battle, it “will save us from the power of our enemies.” They treat God as a charm. The ark is captured, Eli’s sons are killed, Eli falls and dies at the news, and his daughter-in-law, dying in childbirth, names her son Ichabod: “The glory has gone into exile from Israel.”

But the God of Israel does not need Israel to defend him. In the Philistine temple at Ashdod, the statue of their god Dagon is found the next morning “fallen face down on the ground before the ark of the LORD”, and the following morning broken. Plague follows the ark from city to city until the Philistines send it home on a cart. Twenty years later, when Israel at last turns back to the LORD under Samuel, they win a victory at Mizpah, and Samuel sets up a stone and names it Ebenezer, saying, “To this point the LORD has helped us.”

“Give us a king”

Samuel grows old, and his sons are no better than Eli’s. So the elders come to him with a demand: “appoint a king to judge us, as all the nations have.” Samuel is hurt, but God tells him something more painful:

The LORD said to Samuel, “Listen to the people in everything they are saying to you. It is not you they have rejected; it is me they have rejected as their king.

— 1 Samuel 8:7

The request is not wrong in itself. The law of Moses had foreseen that Israel would one day have a king, and Judges ended by lamenting that there was none. The problem is the reason: they want to be “like all the nations”, with a king who will “go out before us and fight our battles”. That was exactly what the LORD had done for them. Samuel warns them what a king will cost: he will take their sons, their daughters, their fields and a tenth of their flocks. They refuse to listen: “we will have a king over us.” And God gives them one.

Saul

Saul is everything the people could have wanted. He is from Gibeah in Benjamin, “a fine young man”, and “from the shoulders up he stood taller than all the people.” Samuel anoints him privately; when he is chosen publicly, he is found hiding among the baggage. His first act as king is a good one: the Spirit of God rushes on him, and he rescues the town of Jabesh-gilead from the Ammonites. For a moment it looks as if the kingdom will be well served.

Then come two failures, and both have the same root. In chapter 13, with the Philistines gathering and his troops deserting, Saul grows tired of waiting for Samuel and offers the sacrifice himself. Samuel arrives as he finishes, and tells him that his kingdom will not last: “The LORD has looked for a man after his own heart.” In chapter 15, ordered to devote the Amalekites to destruction, Saul spares their king and the best of the livestock, then greets Samuel with “I have carried out the command of the LORD.” Samuel’s answer is famous for its dry wit, “Then what is this bleating of sheep that fills my ears?”, and for its verdict:

Samuel said, “Is the LORD as pleased with burnt offerings and sacrifices as with obeying the voice of the LORD? See, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to pay heed is better than the fat of rams.

— 1 Samuel 15:22

The same chapter raises a puzzle readers have long discussed. Twice God is said to regret that he made Saul king (15:11, 15:35), and in between Samuel says that “the Glory of Israel will not lie or change his mind, for he is not a mortal, that he should change his mind.” Most interpreters have taken the two together: God is not fickle or surprised, like a human being who changes course; and yet he is not unmoved by what his people do, and his grief over Saul is real. The chapter holds both, and leaves Samuel grieving too.

The LORD looks at the heart

God sends Samuel to Bethlehem, to the house of Jesse, to anoint a new king. Jesse’s eldest son Eliab is tall and impressive, and Samuel is sure this is the one. The verse at the head of this introduction is God’s reply. Seven sons pass before the prophet, and none is chosen. The youngest has not even been called in. He is out with the sheep.

When David is brought in, God says, “Get up and anoint him. He is the one.” And the book records two movements of the Spirit side by side: “the Spirit of the LORD rushed on David from that day on”, and “the Spirit of the LORD had left Saul.” The rest of 1 Samuel is the long, painful working out of those two sentences.

David and Goliath

The story of David and Goliath has become a proverb for any underdog. In the book itself it is something more specific. The Philistine champion, “about 9 feet 9 inches tall”, has defied the armies of Israel for forty days, and Saul, the tallest man in Israel, the one whose job it was to fight their battles, is afraid. David, sent by his father with food for his brothers, is indignant: “who is he, that he dares to defy the ranks of the living God?”

He refuses Saul’s armour, takes five smooth stones and his sling, and tells Goliath what the battle is really about:

David said to the Philistine, “You have come out against me with a sword, a spear and a javelin. I have come out against you in the name of the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel’s ranks, the one you have defied.

— 1 Samuel 17:45

“The battle belongs to the LORD,” he says, so that everyone will know “that the LORD does not save by sword or spear.” It is Hannah’s song in action: no one wins by strength.

Jonathan

The most moving figure in the second half of the book may be Saul’s son Jonathan. He is a brave warrior, who once attacked a Philistine outpost with only his armour-bearer, saying, “Nothing can keep the LORD from saving, whether by many or by few.” He is the heir to the throne. And from the day he meets David, “Jonathan’s life became bound up with David’s life, and Jonathan loved him as he loved himself.” He makes a covenant with David, gives him his own robe and sword, warns him of his father’s plans, and at last, when David is hunted in the wilderness, goes to find him and “gave him fresh strength in God”. He tells David, “You will reign over Israel, and I will be at your side as your second.” Jonathan gives up a crown for a friend, because he sees that God has chosen him.

Saul’s jealousy and David’s restraint

After Goliath, the women of Israel sing, “Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his tens of thousands”, and from that day Saul watches David with suspicion. More than once he hurls a spear at him. Soon David is a fugitive, hiding in caves and deserts with a band of men who were “in trouble”, in debt or “bitter about their lot”. The priests of Nob who helped him are massacred by Saul’s order.

Twice in these years David has Saul at his mercy, once in a cave near En-gedi and once in Saul’s own camp at night. Twice his men urge him to strike. Twice he refuses:

He told his men, “The LORD forbid that I do this to my lord, the LORD’s anointed, and raise my hand against him! He is the LORD’s anointed.”

— 1 Samuel 24:6

David will not take by force the kingdom God has promised him. He will wait. Between the two episodes, he is about to take bloody revenge on the churlish Nabal when Nabal’s wife Abigail, “a woman of good sense”, meets him on the road and talks him out of it, and David blesses God for keeping him “from taking revenge with my own hand.” The man after God’s heart is not sinless; he deceives a priest, feigns madness before a Philistine king, and lives for a time in the service of Israel’s enemies. But at the decisive moments he trusts God to give what God has promised.

The witch of Endor and Mount Gilboa

Saul’s story ends in darkness. Samuel has died. The Philistines gather for war. Saul inquires of the LORD, “but the LORD did not answer him”. And so the king who had driven the mediums out of the land goes in disguise by night to a medium at Endor and asks her to bring up Samuel. Readers have long debated what happened next: whether Samuel himself appeared, by God’s permission, or something else. The text says that the woman saw Samuel and screamed, and the message is one only Samuel would give: “Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me.”

The next day, on Mount Gilboa, Saul’s sons, Jonathan among them, are killed, and Saul, badly wounded, falls on his own sword. The book ends with one act of honour. The men of Jabesh-gilead, whom Saul had rescued at the start of his reign, travel all night to take his body down from the Philistine wall and bury it.

How to read 1 Samuel

1 Samuel is one of the finest pieces of storytelling in the Bible, and it reads best in long stretches. Read it with 2 Samuel, since the two were once one book. Watch the three main figures, and watch how often the book contrasts them: Samuel’s sons and Eli’s, Saul’s disobedience and David’s restraint, Saul’s spear and Jonathan’s robe. Notice who inquires of the LORD, and who does not wait for an answer. Listen for Hannah’s song as the story unfolds.

The book does not name its author. Chronicles mentions records of the prophets Samuel, Nathan and Gad, and Jewish tradition held that Samuel wrote the part up to his death. Many scholars think the book draws on several older sources and was completed as part of a longer history in the time of the kings or later. Its Hebrew text is also one of the most difficult in the Old Testament, and the ancient Greek translation and the Dead Sea Scrolls preserve readings that differ from it in places. Christians hold a range of views on how the book was composed, while receiving it as Scripture and as the story of how God chose David.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in 1 Samuel are worth knowing before you begin.

“The LORD of Armies.” “The LORD” in capitals stands for God’s personal name. The title that older Bibles render “the LORD of hosts”, first spoken in prayer by Hannah, is translated “the LORD of Armies”.

“The LORD’s anointed.” David’s phrase for Saul is kept word for word: “the LORD’s anointed.” It is the language of Hannah’s song, and the root of the word Messiah.

A gap in the text. The Hebrew of 13:1 seems to have lost a number, and the translation does not guess: “Saul was ... years old when he became king.”

Measures. Ancient measures are given in modern terms, so that Goliath is “about 9 feet 9 inches tall”, the height given in the standard Hebrew text.

Poetry. Hannah’s song in chapter 2 is printed one line per line, as the poetry it is.

Verse numbers. In chapters 21 and 24 the Hebrew verse numbers run one ahead of those in English Bibles; the references in this introduction follow the English numbering.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: 1 Samuel 1
fields.body_html:
Hannah asks the LORD for a son

1There was a man from Ramathaim-zophim in the hill country of Ephraim named Elkanah son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, an Ephraimite. 2He had two wives. One was named Hannah and the other Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah had none. 3Year after year this man went up from his town to worship and to offer sacrifice to the LORD of Armies at Shiloh. The two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests of the LORD there. 4On the day Elkanah offered his sacrifice, he would give portions of the meat to his wife Peninnah and to all her sons and daughters. 5But to Hannah he gave a double portion, because he loved her, even though the LORD had closed her womb. 6Her rival kept taunting her bitterly to upset her, because the LORD had closed her womb. 7So it went on year after year. Every time Hannah went up to the house of the LORD, Peninnah provoked her, and she wept and would not eat. 8Her husband Elkanah said to her, “Hannah, why are you crying? Why do you not eat? Why are you so downcast? Do I not mean more to you than ten sons?” 9Once, when the eating and drinking at Shiloh were over, Hannah got up. Eli the priest sat on his seat beside the doorpost of the LORD’s temple. 10She was in deep anguish, and she prayed to the LORD, weeping without restraint. 11She made a vow and said, “The LORD of Armies, if you will only look on the misery of your servant and remember me, if you will not forget your servant but will give your servant a son, then I will give him to the LORD for his whole life, and no razor will ever touch his head.” 12As she went on praying before the LORD, Eli was watching her mouth. 13Hannah was speaking within herself. Only her lips moved; no sound of her voice could be heard. So Eli thought she was drunk. 14Eli said to her, “How long will you go on being drunk? Get rid of your wine!” 15But Hannah answered, “No, my lord, I am a woman deeply troubled in spirit. I have not been drinking wine or beer; I have been pouring out my soul before the LORD. 16Do not take your servant for a worthless woman. All this time I have been speaking out of my great anguish and distress.” 17Eli answered, “Go in peace. May the God of Israel grant what you have asked of him.” 18She said, “May your servant find favor in your sight.” Then the woman went her way and ate, and her face was no longer downcast. 19Early the next morning they worshiped before the LORD and then went back home to Ramah. Elkanah lay with his wife Hannah, and the LORD remembered her. 20In due time Hannah became pregnant and bore a son. She called him Samuel, for she said,”I asked the LORD for him.” 21Elkanah went up with his whole household to offer the LORD the yearly sacrifice and to pay his vow. 22But Hannah did not go. She told her husband, “Once the boy is weaned, I will bring him to appear before the LORD, and he will stay there for the rest of his life.” 23Her husband Elkanah told her, “Do what seems best to you. Stay at home until you have weaned him. Only may the LORD make his word come true.” So the woman stayed home and nursed her son until she had weaned him. 24Once she had weaned him, she took him up with her, along with three bulls, about 20 quarts of flour and a skin of wine, and brought him to the house of the LORD at Shiloh. The boy was still young. 25They slaughtered the bull and brought the boy to Eli. 26Hannah said, “Pardon me, my lord! As surely as you live, my lord, I am the woman who once stood beside you here, praying to the LORD. 27I prayed for this boy, and the LORD has granted me what I asked of him. 28So I in turn give him to the LORD. All the days of his life he is given over to the LORD.” And he worshiped the LORD there.
fields.summary: Hannah, who has no children, is taunted by her rival and prays in the sanctuary at Shiloh, vowing to give her son to God. Eli the priest blesses her, and she bears Samuel and brings him to serve at Shiloh.

fields.title: 1 Samuel 2
fields.body_html:
Hannah sings to the LORD

1Then Hannah prayed, and she said:
“My heart is glad in the LORD;
in the LORD my horn is raised high.
I boast loudly over my enemies,
because I rejoice in your salvation.
2No one is holy like the LORD;
indeed, there is none but you,
and no rock is like our God.
3Do not keep talking so proudly,
or let arrogant words leave your lips,
for the LORD is a God who knows all things,
and by him every action is weighed.
4The bows of the mighty are broken,
while those who stumbled are armed with strength.
5Those who were full hire themselves out for bread,
but the hungry hunger no more.
The childless woman gives birth to seven,
but the mother of many sons pines away.
6The LORD brings death and gives life;
he sends down to Sheol and brings up again.
7The LORD makes some poor and others rich;
he humbles, and he also exalts.
8He lifts the poor up out of the dust
and raises those in need from the ash heap,
to seat them with nobles
and give them a throne of honor as their own.
For the pillars of the earth belong to the LORD;
on them he has set the world.
9He guards the steps of his faithful ones,
but the wicked are silenced in darkness,
for no one wins by strength.
10Those who oppose the LORD will be shattered;
he will thunder against them from heaven.
The LORD will judge the ends of the earth;
he will grant strength to his king
and raise high the horn of his anointed.”

Eli’s sons treat the offerings with contempt

11Then Elkanah went home to Ramah, but the boy stayed and served the LORD under Eli the priest. 12Now Eli’s sons were worthless men; they did not know the LORD. 13Now this was the priests’ practice with the people: whenever anyone offered a sacrifice, the priest’s servant would come while the meat was boiling, carrying a three-pronged fork, 14and he would plunge it into the pan or kettle or cauldron or pot. Whatever the fork brought up, the priest took for himself. This is how they treated all the Israelites who came there to Shiloh. 15Worse still, before the fat had even been turned into smoke, the priest’s servant would come and tell the man offering the sacrifice, “Hand over some meat for the priest to roast. He will not accept boiled meat from you, only raw.” 16If the man answered, “Let the fat be turned into smoke first, and then take whatever you like,” the servant would say, “No, hand it over now. If you do not, I will take it by force.” 17So the sin of these young men was very great in the sight of the LORD, for they treated the LORD’s offering with contempt. 18Samuel, meanwhile, was serving before the LORD, a boy wearing a linen ephod. 19Each year his mother made him a small robe and brought it to him when she went up with her husband for the yearly sacrifice. 20Eli would bless Elkanah and his wife and say, “May the LORD give you children by this woman to take the place of the one she asked for and gave to the LORD.” Then they would go home. 21And the LORD came to Hannah’s aid: she conceived and bore three sons and two daughters. And all the while the boy Samuel was growing up in the presence of the LORD.

Eli warns his sons

22Eli was now very old. He kept hearing of all that his sons were doing to all Israel, and that they slept with the women serving at the entrance to the tent of meeting. 23He said to them, “Why are you doing these things? I keep hearing from all the people about the evil you are doing. 24No, my sons! The report I hear spreading among the LORD’s people is not good. 25If one person sins against another, God can settle the matter; but if someone sins against the LORD, who can plead for that person?” But they would not listen to their father, because the LORD had decided to put them to death. 26Meanwhile the boy Samuel went on growing up, and both the LORD and the people were pleased with him.

A man of God speaks against Eli’s house

27A man of God came to Eli and said to him, “The LORD says this: ‘Did I not plainly reveal myself to your ancestor’s family when they were in Egypt, subject to Pharaoh’s house? 28Out of all the tribes of Israel, did I not choose him as my priest, to go up to my altar, to offer incense, and to wear an ephod before me? And I gave your ancestor’s family all the food offerings of the Israelites. 29Why do you kick at my sacrifices and offerings, which I commanded for my dwelling? Why do you honor your sons more than me, fattening yourselves on the best parts of every offering made by Israel, my people? 30Therefore the LORD, the God of Israel, declares: I did promise that your family and your ancestor’s family would walk before me forever. But now the LORD declares: That will never be! For I will honor those who honor me, and those who despise me will be treated as nothing. 31The time is coming when I will break your strength and the strength of your ancestor’s family, so that no one in your family will live to old age. 32In my dwelling you will see distress, even while Israel is given every good thing, and no one in your family will ever live to old age. 33Yet one of your descendants I will not cut off from serving at my altar, so that your eyes will fail with weeping and your heart will grieve. All the rest of your descendants will die in the prime of life. 34What happens to your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, will be the sign to you: both of them will die on the same day. 35I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who will do what is in my heart and mind. I will build him a lasting house, and he will walk before my anointed for all time. 36Then everyone left in your family will come and bow down to him for a little silver and a loaf of bread, and say, “Please put me in one of the priestly posts so that I can have a scrap of bread to eat.”‘”
fields.summary: Hannah praises God, who brings low and lifts up. Eli’s sons treat the offerings with contempt, and a man of God tells Eli that his house will be judged, while the boy Samuel grows in favor.

fields.title: 1 Samuel 3
fields.body_html:
The LORD calls the boy Samuel

1The boy Samuel was serving the LORD under Eli. The word of the LORD was rare in those days, and visions were few.

2At that time Eli, whose sight had begun to fail so that he could not see, was lying down in his usual place, 3and the lamp of God had not yet gone out. Samuel lay in the temple of the LORD, where God’s ark was,

4and the LORD called Samuel. He answered, “Here I am.” 5He ran to Eli and said, “Here I am. You called me.” But Eli said, “I did not call you. Go back and lie down.” So he went and lay down.

6Again the LORD called Samuel. Samuel got up, went to Eli, and said, “Here I am. You called me.” “I did not call, my son,” Eli replied. “Go back and lie down.” 7Samuel did not yet know the LORD: no word of the LORD had yet been revealed to him. 8The LORD called Samuel a third time. He got up, went to Eli, and said, “Here I am. You called me.” Then Eli realized that the LORD was calling the boy. 9So Eli told Samuel, “Go and lie down. If he calls you, then say, ‘Speak, LORD, for your servant is listening.’” So Samuel went back and lay down in his place. 10The LORD came and took his stand there, and called as before, “Samuel! Samuel!” Samuel replied, “Speak, for your servant is listening.”

Judgment on Eli’s family

11The LORD said to Samuel, “Look, I am about to do something in Israel that will make both ears of all who hear of it tingle. 12On that day I will carry out against Eli all I have said about his family, from beginning to end. 13I told him that I would bring judgment on his family forever, because of the guilt he knew about: his sons were bringing a curse on themselves, and he did not restrain them. 14Therefore I have sworn to Eli’s family that no sacrifice or offering will ever make atonement for the guilt of Eli’s family.” 15Samuel lay there until morning, and then he opened the doors of the LORD’s house. But he was afraid to tell Eli about the vision. 16But Eli called Samuel. “Samuel, my son!” he said. And Samuel answered, “Here I am.” 17Eli asked, “What was the message he gave you? Please do not hide it from me. May God deal with you ever so severely if you hide from me anything of all that he told you.” 18So Samuel told him everything and hid nothing from him. Eli said, “He is the LORD. Let him do what he sees is good.”

Samuel known as a prophet

19Samuel grew up, and the LORD was with him; he did not let any of his words fall to the ground. 20All Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, knew that Samuel was a proven prophet of the LORD. 21The LORD continued to appear at Shiloh, because there at Shiloh he revealed himself to Samuel through the word of the LORD.
fields.summary: God calls the boy Samuel in the night, and Samuel answers, “Speak, for your servant is listening.” God tells him of the judgment on Eli’s house, and all Israel comes to know Samuel as a prophet.

fields.title: 1 Samuel 4
fields.body_html:
The Philistines capture the ark

1And the word of Samuel reached all Israel. Now Israel went out to meet the Philistines in battle. The Israelites set up camp at Ebenezer, and the Philistines camped at Aphek. 2The Philistines lined up for battle against Israel, and as the fighting spread, Israel was beaten by the Philistines. They killed about 4,000 men in the ranks out on the open field. 3When the troops came back to the camp, the elders of Israel said, “Why has the LORD struck us down before the Philistines today? Let us fetch the ark of the covenant of the LORD from Shiloh. Then it will be among us and will save us from the power of our enemies.” 4So the people sent word to Shiloh, and from there they carried away the ark of the covenant of the LORD of Armies, who sits enthroned on the cherubim. And Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, accompanied the ark of the covenant of God. 5As the ark of the covenant of the LORD reached the camp, all Israel raised such a great shout that the ground shook. 6When the Philistines heard the noise of the shouting, they asked, “What is this great shouting in the camp of the Hebrews?” Then they found out that the ark of the LORD had come into the camp. 7The Philistines were afraid, because they said, “A god has come into the camp.” And they said, “Woe to us! Nothing like this has ever happened before. 8Woe to us! Who will rescue us from the power of these mighty gods? These are the gods who struck down the Egyptians with every kind of plague in the wilderness. 9Be strong, Philistines, and act like men, or you will become slaves of the Hebrews as they have been slaves to you. Act like men and fight!” 10So the Philistines fought, and Israel was defeated, and every man fled to his home. The slaughter was very great: 30,000 of Israel’s foot soldiers fell. 11The ark of God was captured, and both of Eli’s sons, Hophni and Phinehas, died. 12A man of the tribe of Benjamin ran from the battle line and reached Shiloh that same day. His clothes were torn, and there was dirt on his head. 13When he arrived, there was Eli sitting on his seat beside the road, watching, because his heart trembled for the ark of God. The man came to tell the news in the town, and the whole town cried out. 14When Eli heard the sound of the outcry, he asked, “What is the sound of this uproar?” The man hurried over and told Eli. 15Eli was ninety-eight years old, and his eyes were fixed, so that he could not see. 16The man said to Eli, “I am the one who has come from the battle. I fled from the battle line today.” Eli asked, “What happened, my son?” 17The messenger answered, “Israel fled from the Philistines, and there has been a great slaughter among the troops. Your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are dead too, and the ark of God has been captured.”

Eli dies, and Ichabod is born

18As soon as the man mentioned the ark of God, Eli fell backward from his seat beside the gate. His neck broke and he died, since he was old and heavy. For forty years he had judged Israel. 19Now his daughter-in-law, the wife of Phinehas, was pregnant and near the time of giving birth. When she heard the news that the ark of God had been captured and that her father-in-law and her husband had died, she crouched down and gave birth, for her labor pains came on her suddenly. 20As she was dying, the women who stood beside her said, “Do not be afraid; you have given birth to a son.” But she did not answer or pay any attention. 21She named the boy Ichabod, saying, “The glory has gone into exile from Israel.” She said this because the ark of God had been captured, and because of her father-in-law and her husband. 22She said, “The glory has gone into exile from Israel, for the ark of God has been captured.”
fields.summary: The Philistines defeat Israel, capture the ark of God and kill Eli’s sons. When Eli hears the news he falls and dies, and his daughter-in-law names her newborn son Ichabod, for the glory has departed.

fields.title: 1 Samuel 5
fields.body_html:
The ark in the temple of Dagon

1Now the Philistines had captured the ark of God, and they brought it from Ebenezer to Ashdod. 2The Philistines took the ark of God, brought it into the temple of Dagon, and set it up beside Dagon. 3When the people of Ashdod got up early the next day, there was Dagon, fallen face down on the ground before the ark of the LORD. So they took Dagon and set him back in his place. 4Early the following morning they rose, and there was Dagon, fallen face down on the ground before the ark of the LORD. Dagon’s head and both his hands lay cut off on the threshold; only his body was left. 5That is why, to this day, the priests of Dagon and everyone who enters Dagon’s temple in Ashdod do not step on Dagon’s threshold.

6Then the hand of the LORD weighed heavily on the people of Ashdod. He brought ruin on them and struck them with tumors, both Ashdod and the land around it. 7When the people of Ashdod saw how things stood, they said, “The ark of the God of Israel must not remain among us. His hand is pressing hard on us and on Dagon our god.” 8So they sent for all the rulers of the Philistines and gathered them together. “What should we do with the ark of the God of Israel?” they asked. The rulers replied, “Have the ark of the God of Israel taken over to Gath.” So they took the ark of the God of Israel over there.

The ark moved from city to city

9But after they had moved it, the hand of the LORD was against that city and threw it into a great panic. He struck the people of the city, young and old, and tumors broke out on them. 10So they sent the ark of God on to Ekron. But as soon as the ark of God arrived in Ekron, the people of Ekron cried out, “They have brought the ark of the God of Israel over to us to kill us and our people!” 11So they sent for all the rulers of the Philistines and gathered them together. “Send the ark of the God of Israel away,” they said. “Let it go back to its own place, so that it does not kill us and our people.” For a deadly panic had spread through the whole city; the hand of God was very heavy there. 12Those who did not die were struck with tumors, and the cry of the city for help rose up to heaven.
fields.summary: In the temple of Dagon the idol falls before the ark, and the Philistine cities are struck with tumors. They send the ark from town to town.

fields.title: 1 Samuel 6
fields.body_html:
The Philistines send the ark back

1The ark of the LORD was in the land of the Philistines for seven months. 2Then the Philistines summoned the priests and the diviners and said, “What should we do with the ark of the LORD? Tell us what we should send with it when we send it back to its place.” 3They answered, “If you are sending the ark of the God of Israel away, you must not send it empty. Be sure to return a guilt offering to him. Then you will be healed, and you will know why his hand has not been taken away from you.” 4They asked, “What guilt offering should we return to him?” They answered, “Five gold tumors and five gold rats, one for each of the rulers of the Philistines, because the same plague struck all the people and your rulers. 5So make images of your tumors and images of your rats that are destroying the land, and give glory to the God of Israel. Perhaps he will lighten his hand on you, on your gods and on your land. 6Why harden your hearts the way the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened theirs? Once he had dealt harshly with them, did they not let the Israelites go, and they left? 7Now then, get a new cart ready, and two cows that are nursing calves and have never been yoked. Harness the cows to the cart, but take their calves away from them and back home. 8Take the ark of the LORD and set it on the cart, and put the gold objects that you are returning to him as a guilt offering in a box beside it. Then send it off and let it go its way. 9Then watch. If it goes up the road to its own territory, toward Beth-shemesh, then it is he who has brought this great disaster on us. But if not, we will know that it was not his hand that struck us. It just happened to us by chance.” 10The men did this. They took two cows that were nursing calves and harnessed them to the cart, and they penned up their calves at home. 11They set the ark of the LORD on the cart, along with the box, the gold rats and the images of their tumors. 12The cows went straight along the road toward Beth-shemesh. They kept to the one highway, lowing as they went, and did not turn to the right or the left. The rulers of the Philistines walked behind them as far as the border of Beth-shemesh. 13Now the people of Beth-shemesh were out in the valley reaping the wheat harvest. When they looked up and saw the ark, they were glad at the sight. 14The cart reached the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh and stopped there, where there was a large stone. The people split up the cart’s wood and sacrificed the cows to the LORD as a burnt offering.

15The Levites had taken down the ark of the LORD and the box with it that held the gold objects, and had set them on the large stone. On that day the men of Beth-shemesh brought burnt offerings and other sacrifices to the LORD. 16When the five rulers of the Philistines had seen this, they went back to Ekron that same day.

17These are the gold tumors that the Philistines returned as a guilt offering to the LORD: one for Ashdod, one for Gaza, one for Ashkelon, one for Gath and one for Ekron.

18The gold rats matched the number of all the Philistine cities belonging to the five rulers, from fortified cities to country villages, as far as the large stone on which they set the ark of the LORD. That stone is still there to this day in the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh. 19But he struck down some of the men of Beth-shemesh for looking into the ark of the LORD. He struck down seventy men among the people, 50,000 men. The people mourned because the LORD had struck them with such a heavy blow. 20Then the men of Beth-shemesh asked, “Who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God? And to whom should he go up from here, away from us?”

The ark comes to Kiriath-jearim

21So they sent messengers to the people of Kiriath-jearim to say, “The Philistines have brought back the ark of the LORD. Come down and carry it up to your town.”
fields.summary: The Philistines send the ark back on a cart with gifts of gold. It comes to Beth-shemesh, where some who look into it die, and it is taken to Kiriath-jearim.

fields.title: 1 Samuel 7
fields.body_html:
1So the men of Kiriath-jearim came and took up the ark of the LORD. They brought it to the hilltop house of Abinadab, and they consecrated Eleazar his son to keep watch over the ark of the LORD.

2From the day the ark came to stay in Kiriath-jearim, a long time went by, twenty years in all, and the whole house of Israel mourned and longed for the LORD.

Samuel calls Israel back to the LORD

3Then Samuel said to the whole house of Israel, “If you are coming back to the LORD with all your heart, get rid of the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth that are among you. Set your hearts firmly on the LORD and serve him alone, and he will rescue you from the power of the Philistines.” 4So the Israelites got rid of the Baals and the Ashtaroth and served the LORD alone.

The Philistines routed at Mizpah

5Then Samuel said, “Bring all Israel together at Mizpah, and I will pray to the LORD for you.” 6After gathering at Mizpah, they drew water and poured it out in the presence of the LORD. They fasted that day and confessed there, “We have sinned against the LORD.” It was at Mizpah that Samuel judged the Israelites. 7When the Philistines heard that the Israelites had gathered at Mizpah, the rulers of the Philistines marched up against Israel. The Israelites heard about it and were afraid of the Philistines. 8The Israelites said to Samuel, “Do not stop crying out for us to the LORD our God, so that he will save us from the power of the Philistines.” 9Then Samuel took a young lamb that was still nursing and offered it whole as a burnt offering to the LORD. He cried out to the LORD for Israel, and the LORD answered him. 10Samuel was in the middle of offering up the burnt offering when the Philistines drew near to attack Israel. But that day the LORD thundered against the Philistines with a mighty roar and threw them into panic, and they were beaten before Israel. 11The men of Israel went out from Mizpah, chased the Philistines, and struck them down all the way to a place below Beth-car. 12Then Samuel took a single stone and placed it between Mizpah and Shen. He called it Ebenezer and said, “To this point the LORD has helped us.” 13So the Philistines were brought low, and they did not invade Israel’s territory again. The hand of the LORD was against the Philistines throughout the days of Samuel. 14The towns that the Philistines had taken from Israel were given back to Israel, from Ekron to Gath, and Israel freed the land around them from the power of the Philistines. There was also peace between Israel and the Amorites. 15Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life. 16Every year he would make a round of Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah, judging Israel at each of these places. 17Then he would go back to Ramah, since his home was there, and he judged Israel there as well. And he built an altar there to the LORD.
fields.summary: Samuel calls Israel to put away foreign gods, and at Mizpah God throws the Philistines into confusion. Samuel sets up a stone called Ebenezer and judges Israel all his life.

fields.title: 1 Samuel 8
fields.body_html:
Samuel’s sons as judges

1In his old age Samuel appointed his sons as judges over Israel. 2His firstborn son was named Joel, and his second Abijah. They served as judges in Beersheba. 3But his sons did not follow his ways. They turned aside after dishonest gain; they took bribes and bent justice.

The elders ask for a king

4So all the elders of Israel came together and went to Samuel at Ramah. 5They said to him, “You are old, and your sons do not follow your ways. So now appoint a king to judge us, as all the nations have.” 6But Samuel was displeased when they said, “Give us a king to judge us,” and he prayed to the LORD.

7The LORD said to Samuel, “Listen to the people in everything they are saying to you. It is not you they have rejected; it is me they have rejected as their king. 8They are doing to you just what they have always done since the day I brought them up from Egypt: to this very day they have forsaken me and served other gods. 9So now, do as they ask. But you must warn them solemnly and tell them the ways of the king who will reign over them.”

What a king will take

10So Samuel told the people who were asking him for a king all that the LORD had said.

11He said, “These will be the ways of the king who will reign over you: your sons he will take and put to work for himself in his chariots and among his horsemen, and they will run in front of his chariots, 12and he will appoint some for himself as commanders of thousands and commanders of fifties, and others to plow his fields and reap his harvest and make his weapons of war and the equipment for his chariots. 13He will take your daughters to be perfumers and cooks and bakers. 14The best of your fields and vineyards and olive groves he will take and hand over to his officials. 15He will take a tenth of your grain and of your grape harvest and give it to his court officials and his servants. 16He will take your male and female servants, the best of your young men, and your donkeys, and put them to work for himself. 17Of your flocks he will take a tenth, and you yourselves will become his slaves. 18When that day comes, you will cry out because of the king you have chosen for yourselves, but the LORD will not answer you then.” 19But the people refused to listen to Samuel. “No,” they said, “we will have a king over us, 20so that we too may be like all the nations. Our king will judge us and go out before us and fight our battles.” 21When Samuel had heard all that the people said, he repeated it to the LORD.

22The LORD said to Samuel, “Do as they ask, and give them a king.” Then Samuel said to the men of Israel, “Go back, each of you, to your own town.”
fields.summary: Samuel’s sons are corrupt, and the elders ask for a king like all the nations. Samuel warns them what a king will take from them, but they insist, and God tells Samuel to give them a king.

fields.title: 1 Samuel 9
fields.body_html:
Saul looks for his father’s donkeys

1There was a man from the tribe of Benjamin whose name was Kish. He was the son of Abiel, son of Zeror, son of Becorath, son of Aphiah, son of a Benjaminite, and he was a man of wealth and standing. 2He had a son named Saul, a fine young man. No one among the Israelites was more handsome than he, and from the shoulders up he stood taller than all the people. 3Now the donkeys of Saul’s father Kish had strayed and were lost. So Kish said to his son Saul, “Take one of the servants with you, and go and look for the donkeys.” 4He went through the hill country of Ephraim and through the region of Shalishah, but they did not find them. They went through the region of Shaalim, but the donkeys were not there. Then he went through the territory of Benjamin, and still they did not find them. 5When they reached the district of Zuph, Saul said to the servant who was with him, “Come on, let us go back, or my father will stop thinking about the donkeys and start worrying about us.” 6But the servant answered, “Listen, there is a man of God in this town, and he is highly respected. Everything he says comes true. Let us go there now. Perhaps he can tell us something about the journey we have set out on.” 7Saul said to his servant, “But if we go, what can we bring the man? The bread in our bags is gone, and we have nothing to bring the man of God as a gift. What do we have with us?” 8The servant answered Saul again, “Look, I have about a tenth of an ounce of silver with me. I can give that to the man of God, so that he will tell us about our journey.” 9(In earlier times in Israel, anyone who went to ask God for guidance would say, “Come, let us go to the seer.” For the one who is now called a prophet used to be called a seer.) 10Saul said to his servant, “That is a good idea. Come on, let us go.” So they set off for the town where the man of God was. 11As they were climbing the hill to the town, they met some young women coming out to draw water, and they asked them, “Is the seer here?” 12They answered, “Yes, he is. He is just ahead of you. Hurry now; he has come to town today because the people are holding a sacrifice at the high place. 13As soon as you enter the town you will catch him, before he goes up to the high place for the meal. The people do not eat until he arrives, because he must bless the sacrifice; after that the guests eat. Go up now, for this is just the time to find him.” 14So they went up to the town. As they were entering it, there was Samuel, coming out toward them on his way up to the high place.

The LORD shows Samuel the man

15Now the day before Saul came, the LORD had revealed this to Samuel, 16“Tomorrow at about this time I will send you a man from the land of Benjamin. Anoint him as ruler over my people Israel. He will rescue my people from the power of the Philistines, for I have looked on my people, because their cry has reached me.” 17As soon as Samuel caught sight of Saul, the LORD said to him, “There is the man I spoke to you about. He is the one who will govern my people.” 18Saul went up to Samuel inside the gate and asked, “Would you tell me, please, where the seer’s house is?” 19Samuel answered Saul, “I am the seer. Go up ahead of me to the high place, for today you are both to eat with me. In the morning I will send you on your way, and I will tell you everything that is on your mind. 20Do not trouble yourself about the donkeys that went missing three days ago; they have been found. And on whom is all Israel’s desire fixed? Is it not on you and on all your father’s family?”

21Saul replied, “But I am a Benjaminite, from the smallest of Israel’s tribes, and my clan is the least of all the clans of the tribe of Benjamin. Why do you say such a thing to me?”

Saul at Samuel’s table

22Samuel took Saul and his servant and led them into the hall, where he gave them places at the head of the guests, who were about thirty men. 23Samuel told the cook, “Bring the portion I gave you, the one I told you to set aside.” 24So the cook took up the thigh with what was on it and set it before Saul. Samuel said, “Here is what was kept for you. Eat it, because it was saved for you for this occasion, ever since I said, ‘I have invited the guests.’” So Saul ate with Samuel that day. 25When they had come down from the high place into the town, Samuel talked with Saul on the roof. 26They got up early, and at daybreak Samuel called to Saul on the roof, “Get up, and I will send you on your way.” Saul got up, and he and Samuel went outside together. 27As they were going down to the edge of the town, Samuel said to Saul, “Tell the servant to walk on ahead of us”—and he walked on—“but you stay here a while, so that I can give you a message from God.”
fields.summary: Saul, searching for his father’s lost donkeys, comes to Samuel. God has told Samuel that this is the man to lead Israel, and Samuel honors Saul at a meal.

fields.title: 1 Samuel 10
fields.body_html:
Samuel anoints Saul and gives him signs

1Then Samuel took the flask of oil and poured it on Saul’s head. He kissed him and said, “Has not the LORD anointed you to be ruler over his own inheritance? 2When you leave me today, you will come upon two men near Rachel’s tomb at Zelzah, in the territory of Benjamin. They will tell you, ‘The donkeys you went looking for have been found. Your father has stopped thinking about the donkeys and is worried about you. He is saying, “What am I to do about my son?”‘ 3Then you will go on from there until you reach the oak of Tabor. Three men will meet you there on their way up to worship God at Bethel. One will be carrying three young goats, another three loaves of bread, and the third a skin of wine. 4They will greet you and give you two loaves of bread, and you will accept them from them. 5Next you will reach Gibeah of God, where there are Philistine garrisons. Just as you enter the town, you will meet a band of prophets as they come down from the high place. Harp, tambourine, flute and lyre will be going before them, and they will be prophesying. 6The Spirit of the LORD will rush on you, and you will prophesy with them and be changed into a different man. 7When these signs have happened to you, do whatever the moment calls for, for God is with you. 8Then go down to Gilgal before me. I will come down to join you there, to offer burnt offerings and sacrifice peace offerings. You must wait seven days for me to come, and then I will make known to you what you should do.” 9As Saul turned to leave Samuel, God changed his heart, and all these signs came true that day.

Saul among the prophets

10When they came to Gibeah, a band of prophets met him there. The Spirit of God rushed on him, and he prophesied among them. 11When all who had known him before saw him prophesying with the prophets, the people asked one another, “What has come over the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?” 12A man who lived there answered, “And who is their father?” That is how the saying came about: “Is Saul also among the prophets?” 13When he had finished prophesying, he went to the high place. 14Saul’s uncle asked him and his servant, “Where have you been?” “Looking for the donkeys,” Saul said. “When we saw they were nowhere to be found, we went to Samuel.” 15Saul’s uncle said, “Please tell me what Samuel said to you.” 16Saul answered his uncle, “He assured us that the donkeys had been found.” But he did not tell him what Samuel had said about the kingship.

Saul chosen by lot at Mizpah

17Samuel summoned the people to the LORD at Mizpah. 18He said to the Israelites, “The LORD, the God of Israel, says this: ‘I brought Israel up out of Egypt. I rescued you from the power of the Egyptians and of all the kingdoms that were oppressing you.’ 19But today you have rejected your God, the one who saves you from all your troubles and distress. You have told him, ‘Set a king over us instead.’ So now present yourselves before the LORD tribe by tribe and clan by clan.” 20Samuel then brought all the tribes of Israel forward, and the lot fell on the tribe of Benjamin. 21Then he had the tribe of Benjamin come forward clan by clan, and the clan of the Matrites was chosen. Finally Saul son of Kish was chosen. But when they searched for him, he was not there. 22So they inquired again of the LORD, “Has the man come here yet?” The LORD answered, “There he is, hiding among the baggage.” 23They ran and brought him out, and when he stood among the people he was taller than any of them by a head and shoulders. 24Samuel said to all the people, “Do you see the man the LORD has chosen? Among all the people there is no one like him.” Then all the people shouted, “Long live the king!”

25Samuel explained to the people the rights and duties of the kingship. He wrote them in a scroll and placed it before the LORD. Then Samuel sent all the people home. 26Saul also went home to Gibeah, and with him went men of valor whose hearts God had moved. 27But some worthless men said, “How can this fellow save us?” They looked down on him and brought him no gift. But he held his tongue.
fields.summary: Samuel anoints Saul in private, and the signs he foretold come true as the Spirit of God comes on Saul. At Mizpah Saul is chosen by lot and proclaimed king, though some despise him.

fields.title: 1 Samuel 11
fields.body_html:
Nahash threatens Jabesh-gilead

1Then Nahash the Ammonite went up and besieged Jabesh-gilead, and all the men of Jabesh told Nahash, “If you make a treaty with us, we will be subject to you.” 2But Nahash the Ammonite answered them, “I will make a treaty with you, but only on this condition: I will gouge out the right eye of every one of you. In this way I will bring disgrace on all Israel.” 3The elders of Jabesh said to him, “Give us seven days, so that we can send messengers throughout the territory of Israel. Then, if no one comes to rescue us, we will come out and surrender to you.” 4When the messengers came to Gibeah of Saul and told the people what had happened, all the people wept aloud. 5Just then Saul was coming in from the field behind his oxen. He asked, “What is wrong with the people? Why are they weeping?” They told him what the men of Jabesh had said. 6When Saul heard these words, the Spirit of God rushed on him, and he became very angry. 7He took a yoke of oxen and cut them up, and he sent the pieces by the messengers through all the territory of Israel with this message: “Anyone who does not come out behind Saul and Samuel will have the same done to his oxen.” Then the dread of the LORD fell on the people, and they came out as one man. 8When Saul counted them at Bezek, the men of Israel numbered 300,000, and the men of Judah 30,000. 9They told the messengers who had come, “Say to the men of Jabesh-gilead, ‘Rescue will come to you tomorrow, by the time the sun is hot.’” When the messengers went back and told the men of Jabesh, they were glad. 10Then the men of Jabesh said to the Ammonites, “Tomorrow we will come out to you, and you may do with us whatever you think best.”

Saul rescues Jabesh-gilead

11The next day Saul arranged the army in three companies. During the morning watch they broke into the camp and cut down the Ammonites until the heat of the day. The survivors were scattered so widely that no two of them were left together. 12Then the people said to Samuel, “Who were the ones who said, ‘Is Saul to reign over us?’ Hand those men over, and we will put them to death.” 13But Saul said, “No one will be put to death today, for today the LORD has brought deliverance to Israel.”

The kingship renewed at Gilgal

14Samuel then told the people, “Come, let us go to Gilgal and there renew the kingship.” 15So all the people went to Gilgal, and there, in the presence of the LORD at Gilgal, they made Saul king. They offered peace offerings there before the LORD, and Saul and all the men of Israel celebrated with great joy.
fields.summary: Saul rescues Jabesh-gilead from Nahash the Ammonite, and the people renew the kingdom at Gilgal.

fields.title: 1 Samuel 12
fields.body_html:
Samuel calls Israel to witness his conduct

1Samuel said to all Israel, “I have listened to you and done everything you asked of me. I have set a king over you. 2Now the king will lead you. As for me, I am old and gray, and my sons are here among you. I have led you from my youth until this day. 3Here I am. Bring your charges against me before the LORD and before his anointed. Whose ox did I take? Whose donkey? Whom did I cheat? Whom did I treat harshly? From whom did I take a bribe to make me look the other way? If I have, I will pay it back to you.” 4They answered, “You have not cheated us or treated us harshly, and you have not taken anything from anyone.” 5Samuel said to them, “Today the LORD is witness against you, and so is his anointed: you have found nothing in my hand.” “He is witness,” they said.

Samuel recalls what the LORD has done

6Samuel said to the people, “It is the LORD who appointed Moses and Aaron and brought your ancestors up from the land of Egypt. 7So now take your stand, and I will put the case to you before the LORD, recounting all the righteous acts that the LORD has done for you and for your ancestors. 8After Jacob went to Egypt, your ancestors cried out to the LORD, and the LORD sent Moses and Aaron. They brought your ancestors out of Egypt and settled them in this place. 9But they forgot the LORD their God, so he sold them into the power of Sisera, who was commander of the army of Hazor, and into the power of the Philistines and the king of Moab, and these fought against them. 10Then they cried out to the LORD, saying, ‘We have sinned. We have abandoned the LORD and served the Baals and the Ashtaroth. But now rescue us from the power of our enemies, and we will serve you.’ 11Then the LORD sent Jerubbaal, Bedan, Jephthah and Samuel, and he rescued you from the power of the enemies around you, and you lived in safety. 12But when you saw that Nahash king of the Ammonites was coming against you, you said to me, ‘No! A king must reign over us,’ though the LORD your God was your king. 13Now here is the king you have chosen, the one you asked for. See, the LORD has set a king over you. 14If you fear the LORD, serve him, obey his voice and do not rebel against the LORD’s command, then both you and the king who reigns over you will be followers of the LORD your God. 15But if you do not obey the voice of the LORD and you rebel against the LORD’s command, then the LORD’s hand will be against you, as it was against your ancestors. 16Now then, take your stand and watch this great thing the LORD is about to do before your eyes. 17Is this not the time of the wheat harvest? I will call on the LORD, and he will send thunder and rain. Then you will know and see how great is the evil you have done in the sight of the LORD by asking for a king for yourselves.”

Thunder and rain at harvest time

18So Samuel called on the LORD, and that same day the LORD sent thunder and rain. All the people were filled with fear of the LORD and of Samuel. 19All the people said to Samuel, “Pray for your servants to the LORD your God, or we will die! To all our other sins we have added this evil: we asked for a king for ourselves.”

20Samuel said to the people, “Do not be afraid. You have done all this evil, yes; but do not turn away from following the LORD. Serve the LORD with all your heart. 21Do not turn aside to follow worthless things that cannot help you or rescue you, because they are worthless. 22For his great name’s sake the LORD will not forsake his people, because the LORD has been pleased to make you his own people. 23As for me, far be it from me to sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you. I will go on teaching you the way that is good and right. 24Only fear the LORD and serve him faithfully with all your heart. Think of the great things he has done for you. 25But if you go on doing evil, you and your king alike will be swept away.”
fields.summary: Samuel reminds Israel of his own honesty and of God’s faithfulness, and warns that both people and king must follow God. Thunder in the wheat harvest shows the evil of asking for a king, yet Samuel promises to pray for them.

fields.title: 1 Samuel 13
fields.body_html:
War with the Philistines

1Saul was ... years old when he became king, and he reigned over Israel two years. 2Saul chose 3,000 men of Israel for himself. Of these, 2,000 stayed with Saul in Michmash and the hill country of Bethel, and 1,000 were with Jonathan in Gibeah of Benjamin. The rest of the people he sent home, each to his own tent. 3Jonathan attacked the Philistine garrison at Geba, and the Philistines heard about it. Then Saul blew the ram’s horn throughout the land and said, “Let the Hebrews hear!” 4All Israel heard the news: “Saul has attacked the Philistine garrison, and now Israel has become a stench to the Philistines.” And the people were called out to join Saul at Gilgal. 5The Philistines gathered to fight against Israel: 30,000 chariots, 6,000 horsemen, and foot soldiers as many as the sand on the seashore. They came up and camped at Michmash, east of Beth-aven. 6When the men of Israel saw that they were in trouble, because the army was hard pressed, the people hid in caves and thickets, among the rocks, in holes in the ground, and in cisterns. 7Some Hebrews even crossed the Jordan to the land of Gad and Gilead. But Saul was still at Gilgal, and all the troops who followed him were trembling. 8He waited seven days, the time Samuel had set, but Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and the troops began to slip away from Saul. 9So Saul said, “Bring the burnt offering and the peace offerings here to me.” Then he offered the burnt offering. 10Just as he finished offering the burnt offering, Samuel arrived. Saul went out to meet him and greet him. 11Samuel said, “What have you done?” Saul answered, “I saw that the troops were scattering from me, that you had not come within the days you had set, and that the Philistines were gathering at Michmash, 12I thought, ‘The Philistines will now come down on me at Gilgal, and I have not yet sought the LORD’s favor.’ So I forced myself and offered the burnt offering.”

Saul’s kingdom will not last

13Samuel said to Saul, “You have acted foolishly. You have not kept the commandment the LORD your God gave you. Had you kept it, the LORD would now have made your kingdom over Israel secure for all time. 14But now your kingdom will not last. The LORD has looked for a man after his own heart, and the LORD has appointed him ruler over his people, because you have not kept what the LORD commanded you.”

15Then Samuel got up and went from Gilgal up to Gibeah of Benjamin. Saul counted the troops who were still with him, about 600 men. 16Saul and his son Jonathan and the troops who were with them were staying in Geba of Benjamin, while the Philistines were camped at Michmash. 17Raiding parties came out of the Philistine camp in three companies. One company turned toward the road to Ophrah, in the land of Shual. 18Another company turned toward the road to Beth-horon, and another turned toward the road to the border that overlooks the Valley of Zeboim, toward the wilderness.

No blacksmith in Israel

19No blacksmith could be found anywhere in Israel’s land, for the Philistines had said, “The Hebrews must not make swords or spears.” 20So all Israel had to go down to the Philistines to have their plowshares, mattocks, axes and colters sharpened. 21The charge was about 1/4 ounce for plowshares and mattocks, and about 1/8 ounce for forks and axes and for fixing the points on ox goads. 22So on the day of battle, not one of the soldiers with Saul and Jonathan had a sword or a spear in hand; only Saul and his son Jonathan had them. 23Now the Philistine garrison had moved out to the pass at Michmash.
fields.summary: Facing the Philistines at Michmash, Saul offers the sacrifice himself instead of waiting for Samuel. Samuel tells him that his kingdom will not last, and Israel has no swords because the Philistines control the smiths.

fields.title: 1 Samuel 14
fields.body_html:
Jonathan attacks the Philistine outpost

1One day Jonathan son of Saul said to the young man who carried his armor, “Come on, let us go across to the Philistine outpost on the far side, over there.” But he did not tell his father. 2Saul was staying on the outskirts of Gibeah under the pomegranate tree at Migron, and the troops with him numbered about six hundred men. 3Ahijah son of Ahitub was there, wearing an ephod. Ahitub was the brother of Ichabod son of Phinehas son of Eli, the priest of the LORD at Shiloh. The troops did not know that Jonathan had gone. 4In the pass that Jonathan meant to cross to reach the Philistine outpost there was a rocky crag on one side and a rocky crag on the other. One was named Bozez and the other Seneh. 5One crag rose like a pillar on the north side, facing Michmash, and the other stood on the south side, facing Geba.

6Jonathan said to the young man who carried his armor, “Come, let us cross to the post held by these uncircumcised men. It may be that the LORD will act for us. Nothing can keep the LORD from saving, whether by many or by few.” 7His armor-bearer answered him, “Do everything you have in mind. Go ahead. I am with you, whatever you decide.”

8Jonathan said, “All right, we will cross over to the men and let them see us. 9If they say to us, ‘Stay where you are until we come to you,’ then we will stand where we are and not go up to them. 10But if they say, ‘Come up to us,’ then we will go up, because the LORD has given them into our power. That will be our sign.” 11So the two of them let the Philistine outpost see them. And the Philistines said, “Look! Hebrews are coming out of the holes where they have been hiding.” 12The men at the outpost shouted to Jonathan and his armor-bearer, “Come up here to us, and we will teach you a lesson!” Jonathan said to his armor-bearer, “Climb up behind me, for the LORD has given them into Israel’s power.” 13Jonathan climbed up using his hands and feet, and his armor-bearer followed. The Philistines fell before Jonathan, and his armor-bearer, coming after him, finished them off. 14In that first attack Jonathan and his armor-bearer killed about twenty men within an area of about half an acre. 15Panic struck the camp, the open country and all the troops. Even the outpost and the raiding parties trembled. The ground shook, and it became a panic sent by God. 16Saul’s lookouts in Gibeah of Benjamin saw the crowd of soldiers melting away, scattering in every direction.

17Saul said to the troops with him, “Count the men and see who is missing.” When they counted, Jonathan and his armor-bearer were not there. 18Saul said to Ahijah, “Bring the ark of God here.” At that time the ark of God was with the Israelites. 19While Saul was talking to the priest, the uproar in the Philistine camp kept growing louder and louder. So Saul said to the priest, “Hold back your hand.” 20Then Saul and all the troops with him rallied and went into the battle. There they found every Philistine’s sword turned against his comrade, in utter confusion. 21The Hebrews who had been with the Philistines before, and had gone up with them into the camp from the country around, also turned to join the Israelites who were with Saul and Jonathan. 22All the Israelites who had hidden in the hill country of Ephraim heard that the Philistines had fled, and they too joined the battle and kept close on their heels. 23So the LORD saved Israel on that day, and the fighting moved on past Beth-aven. 24The Israelite troops were worn out that day, because Saul had bound the army with an oath: “Cursed be anyone who eats food before evening, before I have taken revenge on my enemies!” So none of the troops tasted any food.

Honey in the woods

25The whole army came into the woods, and there was honey on the ground. 26When the troops came into the woods, they saw honey dripping, yet no one lifted his hand to his mouth, because the troops were afraid of the oath. 27But Jonathan had not heard his father put the army under oath. He reached out with the staff he was holding, dipped its tip into the honeycomb and raised it to his mouth, and his eyes brightened. 28One of the soldiers told him, “Your father made the troops swear a solemn oath: ‘Cursed be anyone who eats food today.’ That is why the troops are exhausted.” 29Jonathan said, “My father has brought trouble on the land. See how my eyes have brightened since I tasted this bit of honey. 30How much better if the troops had eaten freely today from what they took from their enemies as plunder! As it is, the defeat of the Philistines has not been great.” 31That day the Israelites struck down the Philistines all the way from Michmash to Aijalon, and the troops were utterly exhausted. 32The troops pounced on the plunder. They took sheep, cattle and calves, slaughtered them on the ground, and ate them with the blood still in them. 33Saul was told, “Look, the troops are sinning against the LORD. They are eating meat with the blood in it.” He said, “You have broken faith! Roll a large stone over to me at once.” 34Then Saul said, “Go out among the troops and tell them, ‘Each of you bring me your ox or your sheep. Slaughter them here and eat. Do not sin against the LORD by eating meat that still has its blood.’” So that night all the troops brought their oxen with them and slaughtered them there. 35Saul built an altar to the LORD. It was the first altar he built to the LORD.

36Saul said, “Let us go down after the Philistines tonight and plunder them until daybreak. Let us not leave a single one of them alive.” They answered, “Do whatever you think best.” But the priest said, “Let us come near to God here first.” 37So Saul asked God, “Should I go down after the Philistines? Will you hand them over to Israel?” But God did not answer him that day. 38Then Saul said, “Come here, all you leaders of the troops, and find out how this sin was committed today. 39As surely as the LORD lives, who saves Israel, even if the guilt lies with my son Jonathan, he must die!” Yet no one among the troops answered him. 40Then he said to all Israel, “You stand on one side, and my son Jonathan and I will stand on the other.” The troops told Saul, “Do whatever you think best.”

The lot falls on Jonathan

41Then Saul said to the LORD, the God of Israel, “Show the right answer.” Jonathan and Saul were taken by the lot, and the troops were cleared. 42Then Saul said, “Cast the lot to decide between me and Jonathan my son.” And Jonathan was taken. 43Saul said to Jonathan, “Tell me what you have done.” So Jonathan told him, “I tasted a little honey on the end of the staff I was holding. Here I am. I am ready to die.” 44Saul said, “May God deal with me ever so severely if you do not die, Jonathan!” 45But the troops said to Saul, “Should Jonathan die, when he has brought about this great deliverance in Israel? Never! As surely as the LORD lives, not one hair of his head will fall to the ground, for he has done this today with God’s help.” So the troops ransomed Jonathan, and he did not die.

46Then Saul stopped pursuing the Philistines and went back up, and the Philistines returned to their own land. 47When Saul had taken the kingship over Israel, he fought against his enemies on every side: Moab, the Ammonites, Edom, the kings of Zobah and the Philistines. Wherever he turned, he punished them. 48He fought with great courage. He struck down the Amalekites and rescued Israel from the power of those who plundered them.

Saul’s family and his wars

49Saul’s sons were Jonathan, Ishvi and Malki-Shua. He had two daughters; the older was named Merab and the younger Michal. 50Saul’s wife was named Ahinoam daughter of Ahimaaz. The commander of his army was named Abner son of Ner, Saul’s uncle. 51Kish, Saul’s father, and Ner, Abner’s father, were sons of Abiel.

52There was hard fighting against the Philistines all of Saul’s life. Whenever Saul saw a strong or brave man, he took him into his service.
fields.summary: Jonathan and his armor-bearer attack a Philistine outpost, and the Philistines panic. Saul’s rash oath nearly costs Jonathan his life, but the people rescue him.

fields.title: 1 Samuel 15
fields.body_html:
Saul sent against Amalek

1Samuel said to Saul, “I am the one the LORD sent to anoint you king over his people Israel. So now, listen to what the LORD is saying.

2The LORD of Armies says this: I have taken note of what Amalek did to Israel, how they opposed Israel on the road as Israel came up out of Egypt. 3Now go and strike Amalek. Devote to destruction everything they have, and do not spare them. Put them to death, men and women, children and nursing infants, cattle and sheep, camels and donkeys.”

4So Saul called up the army and mustered them at Telaim: 200,000 foot soldiers, and 10,000 men from Judah. 5Saul advanced to the city of Amalek and lay in ambush in the ravine. 6Saul said to the Kenites, “Go, leave, get away from the Amalekites, or I will sweep you away along with them. For you showed faithful love to all the Israelites when they came up out of Egypt.” So the Kenites moved away from the Amalekites. 7Then Saul struck down the Amalekites from Havilah all the way to Shur, which lies east of Egypt. 8He captured Agag king of Amalek alive, and he devoted all the people to destruction with the sword. 9But Saul and the troops spared Agag. They also spared the finest sheep and cattle, the fattened animals and the lambs, and everything that was good. They were not willing to devote these to destruction. Everything that was despised and worthless they devoted to destruction.

The LORD rejects Saul as king
